MBE Growth of Superconductors.title: Digitally-alloyed magnetic topological insulator nanostructures grown via stencil mask molecular beam epitaxy
MBE Growth of Superconductors.authors: Jan Karthein, Max Vaßen-Carl, Lars Maier, Abdur Rehman Jalil, Gion Toehgiono, Josua Thieme, Julian Feldewerth, Benjamin Bennemann, Joscha Domnick, Taizo Kawano, Sosuke Otsubo, René Heller, Jun Ishihara, Detlev Grützmacher, Makoto Kohda, Peter Schüffelgen, Thomas Schäpers
MBE Growth of Superconductors.abstract: Magnetic topological insulator nanostructures are a promising platform for the realization of fault-tolerant quantum computation. For this, such nanostructures need to be embedded into the necessary superconducting architectures. In this study, we demonstrate a method for the growth of magnetic topological insulator nanostructures via molecular beam epitaxy, utilising digital alloying and defining their shapes in-situ by stencil mask technology. Cr-doped (Bi$_y$Sb$_{1-y}$)$_2$Te$_3$ micro- and nanometer-sized Hall bars are fabricated and the magneto-transport properties for various Cr doping amounts and different Hall bar dimensions are investigated at low temperatures. We find indications that the Fermi energy is located inside the bulk band gap, while disorder and charge puddles affect the transport behaviour. Furthermore, we investigate the magnetic properties and discuss the transition from ferromagnetic to paramagnetic behaviour.

MBE Growth of Superconductors.title: High-Quality InSb Nanowires Grown by Molecular-Beam Epitaxy via Precise Catalyst Modulation
MBE Growth of Superconductors.authors: Wenlong Yang, Jiaye Xu, Shuai Yang, Wenyu Song, Haiyan Shi, Donghai Li, Xiyu Hou, Sijun Chen, Ke He, Hao Zhang, Dong Pan
MBE Growth of Superconductors.abstract: Semiconductor InSb nanowires are a major material candidate for topological quantum computation. The nanowires in current devices were mostly grown using metal organic chemical vapor deposition, incompatible with in situ growth of superconductor, a crucial requirement for low-disorder devices. Growth of InSb nanowires using molecular-beam epitaxy (MBE) can address this issue. So far, studies on MBE-grown InSb remain limited due to an extremely narrow parameter window for the growth and reproducibility. Moreover, the use of foreign catalysts can introduce deep-level impurities. Here, we report a self-catalyzed MBE growth of InSb nanowires without those foreign catalysts. We first grow GaAs nanowire stems, and then convert Ga catalyst droplets into In droplets in situ. Axial heteroepitaxial growth of InSb can be realized through the In droplets on top of GaAs stems. We further find that a low flux suppresses radial growth, enabling linear length tuning from 0.8 to 2.6 micrometer with growth time, while diameter stays nearly constant. These InSb nanowires have a pure zinc-blende structure free of twins, stacking faults. Transport measurement reveals an electron mobility near 19000 cm2 V-1s-1. Moreover, the observation of quasi-ballistic transport, quantum dots, and Kondo correlations demonstrates the coherent quantum transport capability of the MBE-grown InSb nanowires. Our work provides a substrate-independent, self-catalyzed route for the controllable synthesis of high-quality InSb nanowires, establishing a robust material platform for high-performance InSb-based electronic and quantum devices.

MBE Growth of Superconductors.title: Data-driven reassessment of lattice matching in ScAlN/GaN heterostructures grown by sputter epitaxy and molecular beam epitaxy
MBE Growth of Superconductors.authors: Atsushi Kobayashi, Takuya Maeda, Thai-Son Nguyen, Huili Grace Xing, Debdeep Jena, Yoshio Honda
MBE Growth of Superconductors.abstract: We reassessed the lattice-matching behavior of ScAlN thin films grown on GaN by constructing a unified dataset from sputter epitaxy, molecular beam epitaxy (MBE), and literature reports. The dataset comprised 197 samples, including 32 MBE-grown and 70 sputter-grown films from our laboratories and 95 literature data points, for which Sc composition, growth temperature, film thickness, polarity, growth technique, and a- and c-axis lattice constants were compiled. The compiled data were analyzed using a neural-network-based surrogate model to extract smooth lattice-constant trends within the experimentally covered parameter range, and these trends were subsequently parameterized by empirical polynomial functions of Sc composition and growth temperature. The lattice-matched Sc composition of ScxAl1−xN to GaN was estimated to be x ≈ 0.10–0.13, which is lower than the conventional value of approximately 0.18 and is only weakly dependent on growth temperature and growth technique. In contrast, the c-axis lattice constant was strongly dependent on growth temperature and decreased at higher growth temperatures. This c-axis contraction, together with the reduced c/a ratio, is consistent with growth-temperature-dependent bond softening and local structural distortion in ScAlN, providing a possible structural link to polarization switching in ferroelectric nitrides.

MBE Growth of Superconductors.title: Epitaxial integration of GaN $μ$-platelets and thin films on metallic TiN using a hybrid approach
MBE Growth of Superconductors.authors: Philipp M. John, Thomas Auzelle, Pierre-Marie Coulon, Blandine Alloing, Ileana Florea, Mikel Gómez Ruiz, Jonas Lähnemann, Lutz Geelhaar, Oliver Brandt
MBE Growth of Superconductors.abstract: We demonstrate the synthesis of epitaxial, self-organized GaN $μ$-platelets on metallic TiN thin films. To this end, we first nucleate self-assembled GaN nanowires with number densities between 0.01 to 300 $μm^{-2}$ by molecular beam epitaxy. Subsequent overgrowth of these seed nanowires by metal-organic vapor phase epitaxy yields GaN $μ$-platelets with corresponding number densities. The platelets exhibit N-polarity and form an ohmic contact to the metallic TiN substrate. By adjusting the growth conditions during the metal-organic vapor phase epitaxy, particularly the carrier gas and precursor ratio, the morphology of the GaN can be controlled across a broad range. Growth under N$_{2}$ carrier gas and with a 1:1 NH$_{3}$/trimethylgallium precursor flow ratio results in platelet ensembles with broad diameter and height distributions. In contrast, employing an N$_{2}$/H$_{2}$ carrier gas mixture promotes the formation of more homogeneous ensembles with narrower size distributions around a diameter of $\approx$2 $μm$. Finally, N-rich growth conditions under H$_{2}$ carrier gas enhance lateral growth, leading to the formation of coalesced GaN layers. GaN grown under these latter conditions exhibits strong near-band-edge emission, accompanied by only weak deep-level luminescence at room temperature.

Superconductor-Semiconductor Interfaces.title: Squeezed Light Generation by Cooper Pair Recombination in a Superconductor-Semiconductor Structure
Superconductor-Semiconductor Interfaces.authors: Sima Buchbinder, Avi Koriat, Alex Hayat
Superconductor-Semiconductor Interfaces.abstract: We theoretically demonstrate squeezed light generation in a compact, electrically driven device utilizing the nonlinear light-matter interaction of Cooper-pair recombination in a hybrid superconductorsemiconductor structure. On the basis of second-order perturbation theory, we developed an effective Hamiltonian which incorporates the electronic component of the interaction as a photon coupling strength coefficient, enabling a model to describe the quadrature squeezing effect of Cooper-pair recombination on the photonic state. We find the squeezing strength to be proportional to the superconducting energy gap squared and device length, as well as increasing with applied voltage. For practical device length, materials and voltage bias, we calculated squeezing values comparable to those of existing squeezed light generation methods when operating below the critical temperature. This theoretically developed concept shows viability for electrically pumped squeezed light generation and can pave the way towards realization of squeezing in compact integrated structures.

Superconductor-Semiconductor Interfaces.title: Optically modulated field-dependent electrical response in a non-collinear antiferromagnet/ferromagnet heterostructure
Superconductor-Semiconductor Interfaces.authors: Adrielson Dias, André José, José Lucas, Rodrigo Cristian, José Holanda
Superconductor-Semiconductor Interfaces.abstract: The interplay among optical, electrical, and magnetic stimuli offers opportunities to control the functional response of spintronic heterostructures. Here, we investigate the field-dependent electrical response of MgO/IrMn$_3$/Py/Au under radio-frequency (RF) excitation, white-light illumination, and direct-current (DC) bias. Under a 20 MHz RF signal with a nominal power of 2 W, the measured voltage in the dark remains at several tens of nanovolts. Upon illumination with approximately 1 W of white light, a pronounced field-dependent feature emerges around 315--320 Oe, reaching 0.9--1.0 $μ$V. The illumination-associated differential voltage is approximately 0.95 $μ$V. A DC current of 1 mA produces a response of approximately 1 $μ$V, while the simultaneous application of RF, DC, and optical excitation increases the voltage to approximately 1.8 $μ$V. Magnetic characterization reveals exchange bias with a blocking temperature near 380 K, while electrical resistance measurements show a pronounced dependence on magnetic-field orientation, consistent with the anisotropic response of the heterostructure. These results demonstrate that the field-dependent electrical response can be modulated through combined optical and electrical excitation, involving magneto-optical interactions and spin-dependent transport phenomena, potentially including spin Hall-related contributions and the magnetic spin Hall effect. This work provides insights into coupled optical, electrical, and magnetic-field effects in heterostructures based on non-collinear antiferromagnets and ferromagnetic layers.

Superconductor-Semiconductor Interfaces.title: Phonon emission due to dc-driven electron heating in a two-dimensional electron gas containing artificial scatterers
Superconductor-Semiconductor Interfaces.authors: Frederik Bartels, Mihai Cerchez, Jan Lange, Dominique Mailly, Klaus Pierz, Hans W. Schumacher, Thomas Heinzel
Superconductor-Semiconductor Interfaces.abstract: We report the observation of phonon-induced resistance oscillations (PIROs) up to order $\varepsilon_\mathrm{ph} = 8$ in a two-dimensional electron gas containing artificial scatterers, activated by electron heating due to an applied dc current which enables phonon emission. Under equilibrium conditions, only two weak PIRO maxima are detectable. The dc current simultaneously generates Hall field induced resistance oscillations (HIROs). A precise analysis of their amplitude, which is modulated by the double resonance with PIROs, dramatically enhances the visibility of the latter compared to the equilibrium case. We identify transverse acoustic phonons with a sound velocity of $s = 3.4$\,km/s as the relevant mode and analyze the oscillatory amplitude modulation in the subsonic regime ($\varepsilon_{\mathrm{dc}} < \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ph}}$) within the theoretical framework of Dmitriev \textit{et al.} At the sound barrier ($\varepsilon_{\mathrm{dc}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ph}}$), where the electron drift velocity reaches the speed of sound, we observe a phase shift in the oscillatory electron-phonon interaction that independently confirms recent experimental findings.

Nanowire Selective Area and Template-Ass.title: Mapping the High-Field Response of Superconducting Nanowire Single-Photon Detectors
Nanowire Selective Area and Template-Ass.authors: Harshit Agarwal, Yueh-Chun Wu, Katyayani Seal, Niels Noordzij, Andreas Fognini, Ronan Gourgues, Gábor B. Halász, Benjamin J. Lawrie, Nirjhar Sarkar
Nanowire Selective Area and Template-Ass.abstract: Superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors (SNSPDs) are increasingly being integrated into cryogenic quantum-sensing platforms that operate in large magnetic fields. Here, the high-field limits of these measurements were probed by characterizing the dark count response of a NbTiN SNSPD at up to 14~T using in situ control of the detector orientation and benchmarking that performance against normal detector operation in smaller magnetic fields. The detector performance is strongly anisotropic: perpendicular magnetic fields rapidly reduce the usable bias-current range, whereas near-parallel alignment enables operation at substantially larger total fields, with a finite operating margin retained to 12~T and measurable dark-count response at the 14~T field limit. The angular dependence is governed predominantly by the perpendicular component of the magnetic field, consistent with vortex-mediated suppression of the superconducting current scale. The same field-dependent current scale also determines the electrical pulse amplitude, linking high-field detector operation directly to readout performance. These results establish a practical route for deploying SNSPDs in multi-tesla quantum-sensing and high-field cryogenic experiments.

Nanowire Selective Area and Template-Ass.title: Direct imaging of plasmonic coupling between gold nanoparticles and one-dimensional van der Waals materials
Nanowire Selective Area and Template-Ass.authors: Ibrahim Tanriover, Arindom Nag, Jong-Ho Lee, Huy Hoang, Haihua Liu, Thang Pham
Nanowire Selective Area and Template-Ass.abstract: Hybrids of plasmonic metals and van der Waals (vdW) materials combine electromagnetic field enhancement with the electronic properties of the vdW component, but the studies reported so far concern two-dimensional layers, and the near field at the metal/vdW interface is generally inferred from far-field measurements. Here we report the plasmonic coupling between Au nanoparticles and a one-dimensional (1D) vdW material, NbS3, and measure the near field at the Au-NbS3 contact directly. NbS3 nanowires and nanoribbons were grown by salt-assisted vapor-liquid-solid growth on graphene-covered TEM grids, and atomic-resolution electron microscopy shows atomically sharp Au/NbS3 interfaces. Photon-induced near-field electron microscopy at 1030 nm shows that an Au particle in contact with NbS3 produces a near field of higher intensity and larger extent than an isolated particle of similar size, and that the hot spot at a contact is excited only when the incident polarization is parallel to the particle-NbS3 axis. Finite-difference time-domain simulations reproduce these observations and quantify the dependence of the coupling on the particle-NbS3 gap, the NbS3 thickness, and the dimension ratio of the NbS3 structure. Size-specific Au nanoparticles on NbS3 nanowires enhance the Raman scattering of rhodamine 6G by a factor of 1.8-4.2 relative to Au nanoparticles alone, with a detection limit of 10^-7 M. These results extend plasmonic metal/vdW hybrids to 1D vdW crystals and establish a multimodal approach that correlates the atomic structure of a metal/vdW interface with its nanoscale plasmonic response.

Nanowire Selective Area and Template-Ass.title: Ion-diode-driven hydrovoltaic generation in in situ grown Te/Ag2Te nanowire networks
Nanowire Selective Area and Template-Ass.authors: Dongmei Liu, Zijun Kang, Yulin Cai, Liujia Liu, Dunren He, Yuan Zhou, Huihui Huang
Nanowire Selective Area and Template-Ass.abstract: We report a hydrovoltaic generator based on a three-dimensional porous sponge integrated with in situ grown Te/Ag2Te-heterostructured nanowire networks. Fabricated via a region-specific in situ reaction, the composite scaffold features a dense network of nanoscale fluidic channels that significantly enhance solid–liquid interactions. Upon infiltration of a 0.5 ml de-ionized water droplet, a 1 cm3 device yields a stable open-circuit voltage of ∼180 mV and a short-circuit current of ∼42.5 μA, substantially outperforming its thin-film counterparts. The device exhibits robust environmental adaptability, with the current output thermally enhanced to 178 μA at 80 °C. Mechanistic investigations reveal that the hydrovoltaic generation is governed by dynamic ionic transport rather than classical static electronic band alignment. Specifically, the marginal Zeta potential difference between Te and Ag2Te breaks the spatial symmetry within the nanochannels, functioning as an electrostatic ratchet. This asymmetry establishes an ion-diode-like heterojunction that actively rectifies hydronium ion (H3O+) migration, thereby translating the surface charge disparity into a macroscopic concentration-driven Nernstian potential for ambient energy harvesting.

Nanowire Selective Area and Template-Ass.title: Establishing Standards for Assessment and Reporting of SNSPD Performance
Nanowire Selective Area and Template-Ass.authors: Ari N. Willner, Alejandro Simon, Reed A. Foster, Francesca Incalza, Ava A. Brule, Philip Donald Keathley, Karl K. Berggren
Nanowire Selective Area and Template-Ass.abstract: Superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors (SNSPDs) can be made sensitive to single photons with near-unity detection efficiency, ultra-low dark-count rates, and sub-nanosecond timing jitter over a broad wavelength range. However, many studies report data inconsistently, often emphasizing a single performance metric without considering overall device performance. This inconsistent data reporting limits the field, as it makes it difficult to determine which device characteristics are most important. Different applications require functionalities that may conflict with one another; for example, longer-wavelength operation may require lower operating temperatures. Moreover, there is no universally accepted metric for defining the figures of merit of an SNSPD. In this work, we amass a dataset representing the state of the art of SNSPD fabrication, including operating temperature, operating wavelength, photon count rates (PCR), and dark count rates (DCR). We fit the PCR curves and suggest using the saturation plateau length to gauge the SNSPD's sensitivity. We then fit the DCR and compare the PCR and DCR. Using this approach, we establish a quantitative framework to determine the optimal biasing condition for a given device and to determine the device's sensitivity at that optimal biasing condition, enabling meaningful comparisons across disparate devices. Additionally, we offer concrete benchmarks for measuring device performance.

Nanowire Selective Area and Template-Ass.title: Field-driven dynamics of chiral three-dimensional domain walls in cylindrical nanowires
Nanowire Selective Area and Template-Ass.authors: David Alvarez, Felipe Tejo, Elias Saugar, Oksana Chubykalo-Fesenko, Roberto Moreno
Nanowire Selective Area and Template-Ass.abstract: Three-dimensional magnetic nanowires are promising building blocks for next-generation spintronic devices, where the dynamics of complex domain-wall textures play a central role. Here, we investigate, via micromagnetic simulations, the influence of chirality on the field-driven dynamics of Bloch-point (BP) and vortex–antivortex (VAV) domain walls in cylindrical magnetic nanowires. We show that BP domain walls possess a coupling between their rotational sense and propagation direction, leading to a pronounced non-reciprocal response. Furthermore, BP chirality strongly influences the recurrence of topological transformations during propagation, determining the number of topology-changing events experienced by the wall. In contrast, VAV walls dynamics are not sensitive to chirality, but the VAV pair dynamically rotates around the nanowire axis. These differences are accompanied by a dramatic velocity contrast: VAV walls move at speeds of the order of 1 m/s, whereas BP walls can approach 1 km/s under comparable applied fields. Our results identify chirality as a key parameter controlling both the topological evolution and ultrafast dynamics of three-dimensional domain walls in cylindrical magnetic nanowires.

Nanofabrication and Cleanroom Processes.title: Effect of TiN deposition temperature on fully ALD TiN/high- κ HZO/TiN stack properties for DRAM applications
Nanofabrication and Cleanroom Processes.authors: Boping Wang, Yang Yang, Xueyang Peng, Yuanquan Huang, Qingxiao Zhu, Guanlin Li, Ruifeng Tang, Zhiquan He, Hongtao Shang, Dongping Qiao, Chuanli Zhang, Xun Yu, Zhenkun Chen, Qianqian Wei, Xuanxi Liu, Cheng Huang, Xiaocheng Huang, Pan Xu, Xiao Long, Pengfei Jiang, Yuan Wang, Wei Wei, Tiancheng Gong, Qing Luo
Nanofabrication and Cleanroom Processes.abstract: Dielectrics with high dielectric constant (κ) are crucial for dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) technology, and Hf1−xZrxO2 (HZO) is a promising candidate. The pursuit of higher DRAM storage density necessitates the move from planar to pillar-type capacitors, demanding fully atomic layer deposition (ALD) TiN/high-κ HZO/TiN stacks for their superior deep-trench filling conformality. This work investigates the influence of ALD-TiN deposition temperature on the electrical and structural properties of the high-κ stack. As the deposition temperature increases from 300 to 400 °C: (1) the zero-bias dielectric constant increases from below 50 to above 60; (2) the leakage current density is suppressed to meet DRAM requirements, accompanied by improved frequency stability; (3) the TiN resistivity and surface roughness are decreased without altering its stoichiometry, accompanied by a denser [111] preferred orientation; and (4) no additional contamination or monoclinic (m) phase is introduced into the HZO, while the oxygen vacancy concentration is reduced and the interface quality is improved. This work provides an essential reference for fully ALD TiN/HZO/TiN stacks, a core enabler for capacitor scaling in next-generation monolithic 3D DRAM.

Nanofabrication and Cleanroom Processes.title: Fabrication and characterization of high-quality Nb/Al-AlO x /Nb cross-type Josephson tunnel junctions utilising CMP-based planarisation techniques
Nanofabrication and Cleanroom Processes.authors: Alexander Stoll, Andreas Reifenberger, Daniel Hengstler, Andreas Fleischmann, Christian Enss
Nanofabrication and Cleanroom Processes.abstract: Josephson tunnel junctions (JJs) are the fundamental building blocks of today's most advanced superconducting electronic components, such as qubits and superconducting quantum interference devices (SQUIDs). Given the ongoing demand for scalability of these devices on the wafer-scale, it is crucial to control the fabrication process as precisely as possible to ensure uniform quality and reproducibility. Today, window-type JJs are often used in the production of DC SQUIDs and while they are reliable and reproducible, they suffer from alignment inaccuracies caused by photolithography and unavoidable parasitic capacitances, thus limiting the energy sensitivity of DC SQUIDs. These problems can be circumvented by producing JJs with cross-type geometry, which allows for smaller junction areas and eliminates parasitic capacitances. Here we discuss the fabrication of Nb/Al-AlO x /Nb-based cross-type JJs, where the trilayer is embedded in sputter-deposited SiO 2 to allow for planarisation of structures and to ensure reliable insulation of the sidewalls of the bottom electrode. Instead of lift-off processes that can require processing times of several hours and potentially produce residual dielectric features along the structure edges that might compromise subsequent layers, we use chemical-mechanical polishing (CMP) for the removal of excess SiO 2 . This reduces the duration of the planarization step from hours to minutes and yields smooth, uniform surfaces with a within-wafer non-uniformity of below 5%. The resulting process achieves a junction yield above 90% across 3 inch wafers. In addition, we discuss the influence of fabrication details on the quality and electrical properties of our JJs with different junction areas down to 1 µm × 1 µm distributed across the wafer and extract the junction specific quality parameters from their IV -characteristics. Across the junctions, the spreads are approximately 1% for gap voltage, below 3% for critical current, below 4% for the subgap-to-normal resistance ratio, and below 1% for characteristic voltage.

Nanofabrication and Cleanroom Processes.title: Highly Reliable Sub-2-nm Hafnia Ferroelectric Tunnel Junction via All-Atomic Layer Deposition Growth
Nanofabrication and Cleanroom Processes.authors: Renhao Xue, Yushi Sun, Ruizhan Yan, Zenghui Chang, Mansun Chan, Deep Jariwala, Xiwen Liu
Nanofabrication and Cleanroom Processes.abstract: Hafnia-based ferroelectric tunnel junctions (FTJs) are promising for post-Moore memories, offering fast, low-power polarization switching and compatibility with the technological maturity of the hafnia platform. Yet nanometer-scale barrier thinning, while desirable for higher speed and energy efficiency, introduces a critical reliability bottleneck. Here, we develop an all-atomic layer deposition (ALD) process for reliable sub-2 nm hafnia FTJs through precise growth and low-roughness interface formation. The resulting devices combine sub-2-V operation with a high breakdown field of ∼12.1 MV/cm, while maintaining stable ferroelectric switching through 1010 cycles without breakdown. Further interface optimization extends the resistance-state endurance toward 1010 cycles, reconciling aggressive barrier scaling with reliable device operation. We further exploit 4-bit nonvolatile multilevel operation to demonstrate an in-memory computing simulation with 95.78% accuracy. By combining the advantages of scaling with high reliability, this work advances hafnia-based FTJs toward high-speed, energy-efficient, and robust memory applications.

Nanofabrication and Cleanroom Processes.title: Controlled Growth and Disorder Mitigation of GaAs1-xSbx/InAs Core-Shell Quantum Wires
Nanofabrication and Cleanroom Processes.authors: Ran Zhuo, Huading Song, Yanlin Wu, Wenlong Yang, Haiyan Shi, Xiyu Hou, Sijun Chen, Zhichuan Wang, Donghai Li, Jinjin Bai, Runan Shang, Hao Zhang, Dong Pan
Nanofabrication and Cleanroom Processes.abstract: We report the growth and transport properties of GaAs1-xSbx/InAs core-shell nanowires. Compared with the well-studied GaAs-InAs system, incorporating Sb substantially reduces the lattice mismatch between the core and shell. Accordingly, both the nanowire crystal quality and device performance improved significantly. Increasing x from 0.15 to 0.35, the density of crystalline defects, such as stacking faults in the InAs shell, decreases by half. Moreover, the field-effect mobility increases from 3850 cm2/Vs to 4800 cm2/Vs, consistent with the reduction of the lattice mismatch. The incorporation of Sb makes the nanowire easier to pinch off via the gate voltage, enhancing the electric field tunability over the nanowire. Magneto-conductance measurements reveal Aharonov-Bohm-like oscillations, suggesting a phase-coherent tubular InAs shell. Our results identify lattice mismatch as a critical disorder source in core-shell nanowires and provide a practical route toward low-disorder core-shell quantum devices.

Nanofabrication and Cleanroom Processes.title: Dynamic Tunneling a Prior Phenomenon to Intermediate Resistive States in Defect Engineered Mn-SrTiO3 RRAM Devices
Nanofabrication and Cleanroom Processes.authors: Gowtham Velpandi, Ishaan Tushir, Durairaj Murugan, Thanumalayaperumal Thirunavukarasu, Ranjith Ramadurai
Nanofabrication and Cleanroom Processes.abstract: Resistive random-access memory devices work under the principle of resistive switching from high resistive state to low resistive state under applied electric field. In this work, 2%Mn doped SrTiO3, devices were fabricated using PLD in which, the defects are engineered such that the conducting filament formation is expected to have two oppositely charged defects: a) presence of Mn3+ dopants, giving rise to a negatively charged Mn and Ti and b) single and double positive oxygen vacancies. This process of two filaments emanating from both the electrodes has shown enhancement in the resistive switching characteristics aiding in forming-free switching that exhibits over 102 as ON/OFF ratio with a memory retention beyond 103 seconds at a low read voltage of 0.1V. All devices demonstrated a stable bipolar resistive switching dominated by conduction filament formation resulting from a synergic effect of oxygen vacancies and the varying oxidation states of Mn based negative defects that propagates toward each other under bias. The formation of defect-based filaments around the bias electrode was evidently observed using XPS of the devices before and after switching. A dynamic tunnelling process is observed as an intermediate process before the conduction filament forms in the SET region and following the snapping in the RESET region. Conduction filaments being heavily doped localizes conduction pathways with a small finite tunnelling barrier gap that are instantaneously formed and ruptures during switching cycles. The dynamic tunnelling behavior gives rise to a tiny spike in current and is observed at the intermediate resistive states which are potential for multi-state usage of these devices. Overall, Mn-STO devices of varying thicknesses show promising retention features and defect engineering offers control over single and/or multi-states memory.

Nanofabrication and Cleanroom Processes.title: Low-thermal-budget solution-processed montmorillonite dielectric for low-voltage 2D electronics
Nanofabrication and Cleanroom Processes.authors: Wenjie Li, Junying Xue, Peng Chen, Yongping Dai, Jing He, Ruihao Tan, Jifeng Ge, Tingyi Xia, Shengqi Wang, Zhaoyang Lin
Nanofabrication and Cleanroom Processes.abstract: Low-voltage and high-performance electronic devices based on two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors demand high-quality dielectrics with efficient capacitive gating. However, it currently relies on specially engineered atomic layer deposition (ALD) of ultrathin high- k HfO 2 and ZrO 2 , or high-temperature vapor-phase growth of 2D dielectrics with post-growth transfer process. Here, we report a facile solution-processed 2D dielectric with an ultra-low thermal budget (i.e., at room temperature), while delivering competitive device metrics (e.g., low operating voltage and small hysteresis). This is enabled by an organic-free colloidal ink of montmorillonite (MTM) in environmentally friendly water solvent, eliminating the need for organic ligands or surfactants and thus the post-deposition high-temperature thermal annealing. Specifically, all-solution-processed MoS 2 field-effect transistors with MTM dielectric exhibit a low operating voltage of 1 V and small hysteresis (down to 1 mV). The solution process is generally compatible with diverse n-type and p-type 2D semiconductors such as MoS 2 , MoSe 2 and WSe 2 . Moreover, the robust and reproducible MTM dielectric enables scalable device integration into logic circuits, including inverters, AND, NOR, and NAND gates, as well as static random-access memory (SRAM). The scalable room-temperature solution-processed 2D dielectric offers a route to all-solution-processed and low-voltage 2D electronics.

Germanium and Sn-Ge Epitaxy.title: Chiral topological phases of proximitized planar germanium
Germanium and Sn-Ge Epitaxy.abstract: We investigate the topological phase diagram of a two-dimensional hole gas in planar germanium resulting from the combination of spin-orbit coupling, proximity-induced $s$-wave superconductivity, and magnetization. The peculiarity of the hole gas is the presence of a Rashba spin-orbit interaction cubic in momentum, possibly coexisting with a linear term, which results in the presence of distinct topological phases with Chern numbers as high as four. We map out the topological phase diagram based on effective single-band models with and without spin, and use input parameters based on a self-consistent Schrödinger-Poisson calculation of a planar germanium hole gas. As a concrete model for inducing magnetization in the hole gas, we consider the exchange interaction coming from the presence of a dilute ensemble of manganese impurities. A topological phase with $C=3$ could be accessible experimentally in unstrained planar germanium.

Germanium and Sn-Ge Epitaxy.title: Composition Driven Band Alignment Evolution in Grafted Si/GeSn Heterostructures
Germanium and Sn-Ge Epitaxy.authors: Pargam Vashishtha, Samuel A. Haessly, Yang Liu, Tsung-Han Tsai, Kushal Dahal, Shui-Qing Yu, Edward K. Huang, Nanditha M. Dissanayake, Zhenqiang Ma
Germanium and Sn-Ge Epitaxy.abstract: Understanding and controlling band alignment in lattice-mismatched group-IV semiconductor-based heterostructures is fundamental to rational band-structure engineering, as it governs the electronic structure and carrier transport in heterointegrated semiconductor systems. Despite growing interest in Si/GeSn heterostructures, the composition-dependent band alignment has not been experimentally established. Here, we experimentally establish the evolution of band alignment in semiconductor-grafted Si/GeSn heterostructures with contents ranging from 8.8% to 12.4% using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and Kraut's core-level method. The valence-band offset increases systematically from ~0.29 to ~0.57 eV with increasing Sn composition, whereas the corresponding effective conduction-band offset decreases from ~0.30 to ~0.12 eV. The observed band-alignment evolution is attributed to an upward shift of the GeSn valence-band maximum arising from enhanced p-p orbital hybridization, reduced bonding-antibonding splitting, and compressive-strain-induced heavy-hole band lifting. These findings establish the experimental relationship between alloy composition and interfacial band alignment in semiconductor-grafted Si/GeSn heterostructures, providing a quantitative framework for rational band-structure engineering in lattice-mismatched group-IV semiconductor heterostructures.

Germanium and Sn-Ge Epitaxy.title: Enhancing valley splitting in Si/SiGe Wiggle Well quantum dots through integrated stressor-gate architectures
Germanium and Sn-Ge Epitaxy.authors: E. S. Joseph, Talise Oh, D. E. Savage, D. S. Stone, DeAnna Campbell, Benjamin D. Woods, Mark Friesen, M. A. Eriksson
Germanium and Sn-Ge Epitaxy.abstract: Engineering large and reproducible valley splittings is essential for the scalable operation of silicon spin qubits. In Si/SiGe quantum dot devices, valley splitting arises predominantly from atomic-scale disorder and is therefore inherently random, motivating approaches that introduce a large deterministic contribution. Strain-assisted Wiggle Wells provide a route to deterministic valley splitting by combining an oscillatory Ge concentration in the Si well with shear strain; however, generating the required strain in a manner compatible with large-scale architectures remains a challenge. Here, we propose patterned stressed thin films as a scalable approach for generating shear strain in the quantum well of Si/SiGe quantum dot devices. Finite-element simulations show that compressively stressed TiN films can generate shear strains exceeding 0.1% at the quantum well, sufficient for deterministic valley splittings of hundreds of $μ\text{eV}$ in strain-assisted Wiggle Wells. We show that this strain can extend across multiple quantum dots and is maintained in realistic gate geometries, providing a fabrication-compatible approach for scaling deterministic valley splitting to quantum dot arrays.

Germanium and Sn-Ge Epitaxy.title: Surface passivation and injection-level-dependent carrier recombination dynamics in strained Ge and Ge-Sn
Germanium and Sn-Ge Epitaxy.authors: Apoorva Rose, Steven Johnston, S. Karthikeyan, Muntasir Mahdi, Ze Zong, Wei Zhou, Mantu Hudait

Germanium and Sn-Ge Epitaxy.title: The importance of shear strain in narrow Si/SiGe quantum wells
Germanium and Sn-Ge Epitaxy.authors: Hudaiba Soomro, Talise Oh, M. A. Eriksson, Benjamin D. Woods, Mark Friesen
Germanium and Sn-Ge Epitaxy.abstract: Several heterostructure profiles have been proposed for Si/SiGe quantum wells, to improve the operation of quantum-dot spin qubits. These structures share a common goal of generating either of the two wave vectors that govern the conduction-band valley coupling, dubbed $k_0$ and $k_1$. Here, we focus on the long-wavelength $k_1$ term that couples valleys when paired with shear strain, and which governs the Dresselhaus spin-orbit coupling. We show that shear strain induced by metal top gates may be enough to activate the $k_1$ valley-coupling mechanism, mitigating the need for "ultrasharp" interfaces, as commonly assumed for large valley energy splittings. We propose a scheme featuring narrow quantum wells that does not require ultrasharp interfaces, but should still provide large deterministic valley splittings (when paired with shear strain), and large spin-orbit couplings and $g$-factor corrections, which are of great interest for experimental implementations.

Germanium and Sn-Ge Epitaxy.title: Noise-protected two-qubit gate using anisotropic exchange interaction
Germanium and Sn-Ge Epitaxy.abstract: Hole spin qubits hosted in germanium quantum dots are promising candidates for scalable quantum computing. The strong spin-orbit interaction can enable fast and all-electrical quantum control. Furthermore, the platform can implement universal quantum control using only baseband signals, which may mitigate the impact of crosstalk and microwave-induced heating. At the same time, spin-orbit interaction gives rise to an anisotropic exchange interaction, whose potential for implementing two-qubit gates has remained largely unexplored. However, the current performance of operating a hole-based quantum computer is mostly limited by dephasing due to low-frequency charge noise. In this work, we propose a two-qubit gate protocol for germanium hole spin qubits operated near the gapless regime. This gate protocol exploits the anisotropic exchange interaction between neighboring spins and utilizes a composite-pulse scheme implemented solely through electrical baseband signals. Using this approach, we predict high-fidelity two-qubit controlled- Z operations that can suppress exchange-energy fluctuations, offering a pathway toward fault-tolerant semiconductor quantum processors.

Germanium and Sn-Ge Epitaxy.title: Impact of multi-dot configurations on electron temperature and double quantum dot latching in gate-controlled qubit devices
Germanium and Sn-Ge Epitaxy.authors: Jakob Walsh, Miriam Schweinböck, Jhih-Sian Tu, Yuji Yamamoto, Felix Reichmann, Lars R. Schreiber, Dominique Bougeard
Germanium and Sn-Ge Epitaxy.abstract: Many currently envisaged scalable architectures for Si/SiGe spin qubit devices utilize gate-controlled multi-dot configurations characterized by their peculiar Coulomb blockade physics. One example is the concurrent use of a single electron transistor (SET) as a charge sensor and as a reservoir for adjacent qubit quantum dots (QD). We find that the SET energy spectrum impacts pulsed gate spectroscopy of the QD when the SET simultaneously acts as the reservoir and the sensor. Then, using the qubit QD as a probe, we quantify how strongly the electron temperature of the SET depends on the applied bias. It surpasses a reference experiment by 100 $mK$ even at 50 $μV$ bias. Our results provide a strong incentive for choosing spin qubit initialization schemes which do not rely on coupling to the reservoir in such devices. Switching to a double quantum dot connected to a single reservoir, a frequent configuration for qubit readout, we finally demonstrate the tunability of the characteristic latching behavior by systematically mapping it in the few-electron stability diagram.

Planar Josephson Junctions.title: Direct imaging of vortex lattices across fractional fillings in two-dimensional Josephson junction arrays
Planar Josephson Junctions.authors: Cequn Li, Austin R. Kaczmarek, Omri Lesser, Maciej W. Olszewski, Katja C. Nowack
Planar Josephson Junctions.abstract: Josephson junction arrays are predicted to host a rich sequence of commensurate vortex lattices. However, direct imaging of these configurations remains limited, while transport measurements cannot resolve the underlying vortex arrangements or how order breaks down. Using scanning superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID) microscopy, we resolve individual vortices and directly image this long-predicted hierarchy spanning filling factors $f$ = 1/8 to 1/2 in two-dimensional Au-Nb Josephson junction arrays, including several states with no discernible transport signatures. At $f$ = 1/4, two structurally distinct vortex orders with 4$\times$4 and 2$\times$4 unit cells coexist, consistent with their energetic degeneracy in the frustrated XY model. Away from commensurate filling, we resolve defect structures tied to the underlying vortex-lattice order: the $f$ = 1/2 checkerboard retains its order around isolated excess vortices and vacancies, whereas the $f$ = 1/3 staircase fragments into domains separated by domain walls. These results reveal how frustration, competing configurations, and defects shape the spatial coherence of commensurate vortex order in engineered superconducting lattices.

Planar Josephson Junctions.title: From Growth to Devices: Oxygen-Controlled Superconductivity in BSCCO Thin Films
Planar Josephson Junctions.authors: Sohini Guin, Ramesh Kumar Guin, Pankaj Bhardwaj, Laxmipriya Nanda, Rajib Sarkar, Dhavala Suri
Planar Josephson Junctions.abstract: Realizing device-compatible high-$T_c$ superconductors requires simultaneous control of oxygen stoichiometry and tolerance to nanofabrication. Here, we investigate sputtered Bi$_2$Sr$_2$Ca$_{n-1}$Cu$_n$O$_{2n+4+δ}$ (BSCCO) thin films and establish a direct link between annealing conditions, oxygen incorporation, and superconducting transport. By independently varying the annealing temperature and duration, we identify an optimal annealing condition of $860\,^{\circ}$C for 3\,h, which yields the highest superconducting transition temperature and the narrowest transition among the investigated samples. X-ray diffraction, electron microscopy, and X-ray photoemission spectroscopy reveal a non-monotonic evolution of lattice oxygen, which governs hole doping in the CuO$_2$ planes and produces the characteristic dome-like dependence of $T_c$ on doping concentration. We further translate these optimized films into micro-devices to assess fabrication-induced effects, via micro-bridges as well as a planar Josephson junction. We demonstrate devices fabricated via both lift-off and focused ion beam (FIB) patterning methods -- proving the fabrication compatibility of these films. Importantly, we demonstrate their air-stability for extended periods of time (2 months). The combined insights offer practical guidelines for integrating cuprate thin films into superconducting electronics and quantum device architectures.

Josephson and Proximity Effects.title: Gatemon qubits based on in-situ ternary InAsSb/Al nanowire Josephson junctions
Josephson and Proximity Effects.authors: Zhenhai Sun, David Feldstein-Bofill, Sangeeth Kallatt, Sabbir A. Khan, Morten Kjaergaard
Josephson and Proximity Effects.abstract: Ternary InAsSb/Al nanowires combine compositionally engineerable semiconductor properties with epitaxial proximity superconductivity, making them attractive for hybrid quantum circuits and mesoscopic superconductivity. Here, we realize gatemon qubits based on shadow-defined in-situ InAsSb/Al Josephson junctions in a single growth process. Gate-dependent microwave spectroscopy demonstrates electrostatic tuning of the qubit transition over several gigahertz. Rabi oscillations and Ramsey interference show coherent qubit control, with representative values T1 = 0.79 us and T2* = 0.91 us. Across five gatemons distributed over three chips, the measured relaxation times range from approximately 0.2 us to 1 us and decrease with increasing qubit frequency. Their magnitude is comparable to a circuit estimate of spontaneous emission into the electromagnetic environment. These results establish in-situ InAsSb/Al junctions as coherent, gate-tunable circuit elements and introduce cQED architecture as a microwave probe of the dynamics of the ternary weak link.

Josephson and Proximity Effects.title: A superconducting quantum point contact in Ge
Josephson and Proximity Effects.authors: Anna Tacchini, Inga Seidler, Isabell Grandt-Ionita, Thibault Thuegaz, Stephen W. Bedell, Fabrizio Nichele
Josephson and Proximity Effects.abstract: Hybrid superconducting-semiconducting circuits provide a versatile platform for investigating coherent transport in mesoscopic weak links. Superconducting quantum point contacts (SQPCs) are particularly interesting in this context, as their supercurrent is carried by a discrete number of ballistic transport modes. Here, we investigate a gate-tunable superconducting quantum point contact realized in Ge/SiGe. By incorporating the QPC into a highly asymmetric superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID), we gain access to its current-phase relation (CPR) and switching current, enabling phase-sensitive studies of few-mode superconducting transport. We observe a direct correspondence between conductance quantization and switching-current quantization, linking the normal-state transport modes to the superconducting response. In addition, we demonstrate strong gate tunability of the effective transmission near the onset of the first conductance plateau. Under microwave irradiation, the QPC exhibits photon-assisted multiple Andreev reflections at lower transparencies and Shapiro replicas in the high-transparency, few-mode regime.

Josephson and Proximity Effects.title: Probing synthetic Caroli-de Gennes-Matricon states through critical current in full-shell nanowire Josephson junctions
Josephson and Proximity Effects.authors: Carlos Payá, Ángel Ibabe, Mario Gómez, Thomas Kanne, Jesper Nygård, Ramón Aguado, Pablo San-Jose, Eduardo J. H. Lee, Elsa Prada

Josephson and Proximity Effects.title: Gate-tunable supercurrent switching in a three-terminal quantum dot transistor
Josephson and Proximity Effects.authors: David Novák, Kacper Wrześniewski, Filip Krizek, Wolfgang Belzig, Peter Zalom
Josephson and Proximity Effects.abstract: We propose and analyze a three-terminal superconducting transistor switch in which a gate-defined quantum dot region interrupts a flux-controlled loop. The output supercurrent is switched off completely when the two loop arms couple to the dot with equal tunneling strengths and half a flux quantum threads the loop. The device then operates as a symmetric SQUID at half flux. The condition follows from a single geometric factor $χ$, which reduces the three-terminal problem to an equivalent two-terminal Anderson impurity model and makes the switching mechanism independent of the Coulomb interaction, the dot level position, the total hybridization and temperature. These enter only through a prefactor and thus decide how tolerant the device is to imperfect barrier tuning. Numerical renormalization group calculations across the full coupling parameter space show that the resonance is embedded in a broad region of elevated switching ratio at intermediate hybridization $Γ\approx Δ$, while both weaker and stronger coupling reduce it to a thin isolated line. Finite temperature smooths the underlying singlet-doublet transition and lowers the supercurrent amplitude, but affects the open and closed states comparably and leaves the switching ratio largely intact. Within a zero-bandwidth two-level model, a second dot level is shown to open a leakage channel that grows as the two levels approach in energy. Raising the output barrier and the realistic presence of inter-level Coulomb repulsion, however, suppress the leakage.

Josephson and Proximity Effects.title: Nitride crystalline barrier epitaxial SIS Josephson junctions by MBE
Josephson and Proximity Effects.authors: Manas Verma, Anand Ithepalli, Amit Rohan Rajapurohita, Eegene Clara Chung, David A. Garcia-Wetten, Naomi Pieczulewski, Danqing Wang, John G. Wright, Archit Shah, Jimy Encomendero, Rishabh Singh, Chandrashekar Savant, Hangwang Yang, Anthony Hyatt, Jaehong Choi, Thomas Varghese, Kushagra Aggarwal, Paul B. Welander, Apurva Mehta, David Schuster, Valla Fatemi, Gregory D. Fuchs, Michael C. Hamilton, Hong X. Tang, David A. Muller, Huili Grace Xing, Debdeep Jena
Josephson and Proximity Effects.abstract: Superconductor-insulator-superconductor Josephson junctions with crystalline tunnel barriers have remained elusive by epitaxial techniques such as MOCVD or MBE that produce the junction materials and devices powering today's electronic and photonic systems like transistors and lasers. Here, we overcome the key materials hurdle to realize the first functional nitride crystalline barrier Josephson junctions by MBE. Despite an AlN barrier thickness of approximately 4.5 nm, the NbN/AlN/NbN trilayers exhibit coherent Josephson tunneling with critical current densities of approximately 17 A/cm2, an IcRn product of approximately 2.5 mV, and a superconducting gap voltage of approximately 3.7 mV with a BCS-like gap evolution with temperature. Hysteretic current-voltage characteristics and Fraunhofer current modulation with magnetic field establish underdamped SIS Josephson behavior. The realization of crystalline barrier Josephson junctions by MBE opens the doors to a richer materials palette with alloys and superlattice electrodes and tunnel barriers, as well as potential monolithic integration of superconducting quantum circuits with active electronic and photonic devices such as HEMTs and lasers.

Josephson and Proximity Effects.title: Tunable coupling between valley and magnetic excitons in WS2/CrSBr heterostructures
Josephson and Proximity Effects.authors: Jianchen Dang, Liza Godziashvili, Kaichen Xie, Arun Ramanathan, Vadym Kulichenko, Alejandro Busto, Jia-Yi Ji, Robert Boyd, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Sina Najmaei, Daniel Rhodes, Luis Balicas, Xavier Roy, Ting Cao, Xiao-Xiao Zhang
Josephson and Proximity Effects.abstract: Interfacial coupling in van der Waals two-dimensional (2D) heterostructures offers an effective route to tailor the electronic, optical, and magnetic properties of materials. Versatile control and precise engineering of such interlayer interactions can be further achieved through external parameters, like electric field, magnetic field, optical excitation, as well as layer stacking geometries. Here, we examined the magneto-optical properties of 2D semiconductor heterostructures made of antiferromagnetic CrSBr and a monolayer WS2, both of which host intriguing excitonic properties. We identified a type-II band alignment between these two layers and the magnetic proximity effects from CrSBr, manifested by an enhanced Zeeman valley splitting in the WS2 layer. The interlayer charge transfer shows strong spin selectivity and is governed by the relative alignment between the valley-spin polarization of photoexcited carriers in WS2 and the magnetization in CrSBr, giving rise to spin-sensitive circularly polarized photoluminescence (PL) from WS2. Furthermore, the highly anisotropic electronic dispersion in CrSBr enables stacking-dependent control of interlayer interactions, as inferred from a twist-angle dependence of PL quenching. Our work establishes a highly tunable 2D system that integrates valleytronics and magnetic excitons through multiple coupling channels, opening up new opportunities in all-optical manipulation of spin and magnon states and for the development of flexible spin-optoelectronic devices.

Josephson and Proximity Effects.title: Fermi-arc-mediated transport in surface Josephson junctions of Weyl semimetals
Josephson and Proximity Effects.authors: Rekha Kumari, Dibya Kanti Mukherjee, Arijit Kundu

Josephson and Proximity Effects.title: Mimicking the zero-field Josephson diode effect with remanent magnetization and self-field
Josephson and Proximity Effects.authors: Nathan Satchell, Arjun Sapkota, Pukar Sedai, Kurt Lorenzen, Juan Gomez
Josephson and Proximity Effects.abstract: A Josephson junction whose critical current is larger in one direction than in the other is a diode. With a magnetized barrier, a junction can be a diode at zero applied field, and this is commonly attributed to an intrinsic Josephson diode effect, in which the magnetic barrier breaks time-reversal symmetry. Here we show that the same signatures arise from two ordinary ingredients: the magnetic field of the bias current in the electrodes and the remanent magnetization of the barrier. In cross-type Nb/Pd$_{89}$Ni$_{11}$/Nb junctions, the self-field displaces the interference patterns of the two current polarities in opposite directions. An in-plane remanent magnetization translates the pattern and brings the resulting asymmetry to zero field, where the junction mimics a nonvolatile diode with an asymmetry of 10 to 12% and a polarity set by the magnetization direction. Reversing the current or the field cannot distinguish this mimic from an intrinsic effect, but the wiring can: moving the current lead to the other arm of the electrode across the field reverses the self-field diode, in applied field and at zero field alike, whereas an intrinsic diode would be unchanged. This gives a simple dc test for Josephson diodes in the current-perpendicular-to-plane geometry.

Josephson and Proximity Effects.title: Hidden Spin-Supercurrent Counterflow in Conventional Superconductors
Josephson and Proximity Effects.abstract: Resistive spin currents conventionally vary in space through spin relaxation or torque, which removes angular momentum from the transported spin. We here demonstrate a qualitatively different mechanism in a conventional superconductor exposed to a spin-splitting field. Spin injection across a spin-mixing interface activates a spin-supercurrent contribution, allowing the resistive spin current to vary spatially while the total spin current remains conserved. Even without a net spin-bias across the superconductor, finite and oppositely directed resistive and condensate spin currents arise. This produces a hidden spin-supercurrent counterflow with vanishing total spin and charge currents. The mechanism persists away from exact compensation and remains sizable over broad parameter ranges. The counterflow may be accessible through spin-to-charge conversion, either as a modification of the electrical response of spin-Hall injectors or through a local quasiparticle inverse spin-Hall signal. Our results establish condensate-mediated spin-current compensation as a previously overlooked alternative to spin relaxation.

Josephson and Proximity Effects.title: Achiral-Chiral Dissociation and Structural Zero of the Current in the Spinterface Model of CISS
Josephson and Proximity Effects.abstract: We study the transport sector of the spinterface model of chirality-induced spin selectivity (CISS) under spin-resolved dissipation, extending the quantum non-equilibrium Green's function formulation of Ref.~\cite{Alwan2026QSpinterface} to spin-resolved lead broadenings. The spin current decomposes into an achiral part, driven by the interfacial moment, and a chiral part, driven by the Rashba spin flip. Under increasing lead spin asymmetry, the achiral part grows linearly while the chiral part follows the geometric-mean suppression, so the two sectors dissociate; they also peak at different coupling scales along the lead broadening. The coupling and bias optima are operating points of the reference configuration, not universal scaling laws. A structural zero appears at $λ_R\sin(φ/2)=t_{\mathrm{mol}}$ in the collinear-lead configuration, where the chiral signal collapses to machine precision universally across chain lengths, frequency resolutions, and twist angles; the zero originates from the rank-one singular bond matrix, whose null eigenvector traps an electron in a spin-superposition dark state that does not hop. With non-collinear ferromagnetic leads, the zero is broken in a controlled way: the residual is generically linear in the transverse polarization, arising from a single coherent spin flip at a boundary, and becomes quadratic at a tuned cancellation angle where two boundary contributions interfere destructively, with the scaling exponent jumping sharply from one to two. These results establish the spinterface model as a transport platform with a two-axis dissociation structure, non-scaling operating optima, and an exact structural zero whose non-collinear deformation is a clean linear-plus-quadratic hierarchy.

Josephson and Proximity Effects.title: Cation-intermixing driven evolution from a narrow avoided crossing to an enlarged inverted gap in Ge$_2$Bi$_2$Te$_5$
Josephson and Proximity Effects.authors: Alexander S. Frolov, Alexander V. Fedorov, Nadezhda V. Vladimirova, Sergey M. Aksenov, Mark A. Naumov, Savely V. Domenko, Artem A. Minaev, Vasily S. Stolyarov, Denis V. Vyalikh, Lada V. Yashina
Josephson and Proximity Effects.abstract: Combining the building blocks and structural motifs of the topological insulator Bi$_2$Te$_3$ and the ferroelectric Rashba semiconductor GeTe, we synthesized and comprehensively characterized the resulting Ge$_2$Bi$_2$Te$_5$ compound, which exhibits pronounced cation intermixing. Using momentum-resolved photoemission spectroscopy and ab initio calculations, we demonstrate how cation intermixing drives the evolution of its electronic structure from a narrow avoided crossing to a substantially enlarged inverted band gap. We establish the microscopic origin of this behavior in the redistribution of Ge and Bi atoms within the cation sublattice, which increases the contribution of Bi-derived states near the valence-band maximum and enhances the effective contribution of spin-orbit coupling, thereby stabilizing the topological electronic structure. Our findings demonstrate that cation disorder, which can be controlled during crystal growth, provides an additional degree of freedom for engineering topological electronic structures, opening new opportunities for the development of functional quantum materials.

Josephson and Proximity Effects.title: A discrete realization of the boundary sine-Gordon model and the Schmid transition
Josephson and Proximity Effects.authors: Nicolas Paris, Oscar Bouverot-Dupuis, Christophe Mora
Josephson and Proximity Effects.abstract: The phase diagram of the boundary sine-Gordon model (bsG), or equivalently of the resistively shunted Josephson junction, has been the subject of recent debate. We introduce a discrete model that reproduces exactly the properties of the bsG model and can be simulated extremely efficiently using cluster Monte Carlo algorithms. This enables us to explore a broad range of parameters and compute the complete universal crossover between the weak- and strong-tunneling regimes. We establish the self-duality of the model and unambiguously identify the vertical line of critical fixed points characteristic of the Schmid transition, recovering the conformal field theory predictions along this line with high accuracy. We further clarify the essential distinctions between the Schmid and Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transitions. Our results definitively establish the existence and nature of the Schmid transition and demonstrate the validity of the Schmid-Bulgadaev scenario.

Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.title: Measurement of Parity-Dependent Energy-Phase Relations in a Potential Artificial Kitaev Chain Utilizing a Transmon Qubit
Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.authors: Enna Zhuo, Xiaozhou Yang, Yuyang Huang, Zhaozheng Lyu, Ang Li, Bing Li, Yunxiao Zhang, Xiang Wang, Duolin Wang, Yukun Shi, Anqi Wang, Erik P. A. M. Bakkers, Xiaodong Han, Bingbing Tong, Ziwei Dou, Peiling Li, Guangtong Liu, Xiaohui Song, Fanming Qu, Jie Shen, Li Lu
Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.abstract: Artificial Kitaev chains have emerged as a promising platform for realizing topological quantum computing. Once the chains are formed and Majorana zero modes are braided/fused, reading out the parity of the chains is essential for verifying the non-Abelian property of Majorana zero modes. Here, we demonstrate a transmon-based microwave probe for a four-site quantum dot–superconductor chain based on a Ge/Si nanowire. One end of the chain is incorporated into a superconducting transmon circuit, enabling spectroscopic identification of the chain’s singlet/doublet ground state and thereby inference of its total Fermion parity. We also demonstrate that, for multiple-dot chains, there are two types of 0−π transitions between different charging states: the parity-flip 0−π transition and the parity-preserved 0−π transition. Furthermore, we demonstrate electrostatic tunability of the interdot coupling. This phase-sensitive microwave platform provides a tool for studying complex hybrid superconducting quantum dot systems and for future extended artificial Kitaev chains.

Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.title: Connate Topological Superconductivity and Vortex-Position-Controlled Majorana Modes in the Intergrowth Superconductor Th$_2$Mo$_2$Ir$_2$Si$_4$C
Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.authors: Jiayang Li, Qing Wang, Xun-Jiang Luo, Mingliang Tian, Ning Hao
Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.abstract: The recently synthesized intergrowth compound Th$_2$Mo$_2$Ir$_2$Si$_4$C is an experimentally established bulk superconductor whose topological electronic structure remains unexplored. Here, we identify it as a candidate for connate topological superconductivity and reveal two microscopic routes to vortex Majorana zero modes. First-principles and tight-binding-model calculations uncover Mo--Th band inversion and helical surface states enabled by interorbital spin--orbit coupling between Mo--d$_{xz/yz}$ and Th--d$_{x^2-y^2}$ orbitals. Vortex Bogoliubov--de Gennes calculations further establish a relatively robust surface-state-associated Kitaev phase and a weakly gapped, Th-orbital-derived Kitaev phase. For the latter, shifting the vortex core closes and reopens the vortex-line gap and reverses its one-dimensional topological invariant, consistent with an effective Kitaev-chain mass inversion. Finite-length-vortex calculations reveal distinct spatial and spin-resolved signatures of their Majorana end modes. The orbital Kitaev phase can also exist without helical surface states in a modified model. Although the small orbital-derived gap limits quantitative predictions of experimental observability in this compound, the uncovered mechanism suggests a route to Majorana vortices in multiorbital superconductors beyond the conventional surface-state scenario.

Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.title: Floquet first- and higher-order topological superconductors: A review
Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.authors: Debashish Mondal, Arnob Kumar Ghosh, Arijit Saha, Tanay Nag
Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.abstract: The current developments in quantum technologies are deeply rooted in quantum computation, with Majorana fermions and their topological protection expected to play a central role. In this context, topological superconductors (TSCs) provide a promising platform for investigating Majorana modes and their potential applications in topological quantum computation. In dimensions $d > 1$, the spatial localization of topological Majorana modes can be controlled in higher-order topological superconductors (HOTSCs), extending beyond the conventional framework of first-order topological superconductors (FOTSCs). In this review, we systematically survey the diverse landscape of topological superconductivity, ranging from FOTSCs to third-order topological superconductors (TOTSCs), in which the spatial dimensionality of Majorana zero modes (MZMs) is progressively reduced. We demonstrate how periodic driving protocols enable Floquet engineering of all these phases, even when the corresponding undriven systems are topologically trivial. Furthermore, we investigate various driving schemes and explore the interplay among spin-orbit coupling, magnetic fields, magnetic impurities, and symmetry-breaking mass terms in realizing Floquet higher-order topological superconducting (FHOTSC) phases, characterized by appropriate topological invariants. We also provide an extensive discussion of topological invariants capable of distinguishing conventional MZMs from anomalous Majorana $pi$-modes, which emerge at two distinct quasienergies and have no static counterparts.

Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.title: Reflection Zeros Set the Scattering Invariant of Finite Majorana Wires
Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.abstract: Majorana modes, zero-energy excitations of superconducting wires that are their own antiparticles, could store quantum information protected from local noise. In transport experiments, however, ordinary bound states mimic their signature, a conductance peak at zero voltage, and whether Majorana modes have been observed remains debated. A sign, $Q$, of the electron reflection at zero energy marks the topological phase of a long wire, but what $Q$ certifies in a finite device has been unclear. Here we show for the first time that $Q$ counts reflectionless states, waves that enter through one contact and leave entirely through the other: $Q=-1$ when an odd number of them lie in the lower half of the complex energy plane. In a finite wire this means that the two Majorana modes are split by less than their coupling to the contacts. With equal contacts, every sign change of $Q$, including the bulk topological transition, is an exceptional point at which two such states merge and transmission is maximally flat. At zero temperature, $Q=-1$ exactly when the zero-bias conductance measured at a contact exceeds $e^2/h$. These results show what transport can certify about a Majorana device and how to read the invariant from conductance.

Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.title: Quantum Fluctuations drive Emerging Bosonic Quantum Phases in a Moiré Flatband Superconductor
Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.authors: Yu Hong, Haiming Sun, Qixing Zhang, Le Liu, Zitian Pan, Jundong Zhu, Jingwei Dong, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Luojun Du, Dongxia Shi, Adrian Bachtold, Haiwen Liu, Guangyu Zhang, Wei Yang
Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.abstract: Quantum fluctuations play a central role in superconductors by mediating the interactions that promote electron pairing and controlling the phase coherence required for macroscopic condensation. Thus far, understanding the interplay between quantum fluctuations and superconductivity remains challenging in unconventional superconductors. Here, we establish quantum phase fluctuations as the organizing principle linking superconductivity and Bose-insulating quantum criticality in a moiré flatband superconductor of alternating twisted trilayer graphene (ATTG). Superconductivity is optimal near half-filling of the moiré flatband and gives way to a density-wave-like resistance peak at high temperatures, in which we observe distinct temperature scales for the pairing (~6 K) and the condensation (~1 K). We observe compelling evidence of a bosonic superconducting quantum phase transition, driven by both out-of-plane and in-plane magnetic fields, with a universal critical resistivity of $R_c =~0.62R_Q$ and finite-temperature scaling of $zν_B = 2.3$, where $R_Q = h/4e^2$ is the quantum resistance for bosons. Strikingly, the observed bosonic insulator shows a nearly quantized resistivity of $R_Q$ that saturates at low temperatures and high magnetic fields, together with a zero-bias peak, a nearly zero Hall resistance, and a logarithmic dependence at higher temperatures. Both the superconductor and the bosonic insulator could be driven into the same critical quantum fluctuation regime dynamically under a large bias. Our results establish moiré flatband as a clean platform for studying unconventional superconductivity and bosonic quantum criticality governed by quantum fluctuations.

Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.title: Lattice Commensurability and Majorana sectors of Pfaffian--Anti-Pfaffian interfaces
Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.abstract: We study Pfaffian and anti-Pfaffian non-Abelian fractional quantum anomalous Hall states in half-filled moiré lattice systems. Owing to crystal-momentum conservation modulo a reciprocal lattice vector, these lattice systems admit coupled-wire constructions of the two phases without requiring spatially varying magnetic-field-induced momentum shifts. For the resulting Pfaffian--anti-Pfaffian interface, a Umklapp process can gap the counter-propagating charge sector, while the remaining four co-propagating Majorana modes naturally group into two sectors organized by translation symmetries. Our results show that lattice commensurability qualitatively changes the coupled-wire accessibility of non-Abelian states while providing a microscopic momentum structure that directly constrains their edge and interface dynamics.

Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.title: Evidence of anisotropic surface state residual loss in UTe$_2$ amid isotropic low-energy excitations
Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.authors: Arthur Carlton-Jones, Jared Z. Dans, Gicela Saucedo Salas, Shanta R. Saha, Johnpierre Paglione, Nicholas P. Butch, Steven M. Anlage
Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.abstract: We explore the pairing mechanism and possible topological properties of the unconventional superconductor UTe$_2$ through their influence on both the inductive and resistive channels using resonant cavity perturbation techniques. We measure a composite surface impedance for a variety of UTe$_2$ single crystals at microwave frequencies, where the inductive and resistive channels are comparable and can be treated on equal footing. By studying the composite electrodynamics for a large number of resonant modes, we are able to provide a comprehensive picture of the directional dependence of the excitations out of the ground state. We find similar power-law temperature dependencies at low-temperature for both the penetration depth and surface resistance, which in aggregate across modes, are quadratic and isotropic. On the other hand, we find a distinct and systematic anisotropy of the residual loss. The power-law results are inconsistent with a single pair of point nodes on the Fermi surface under weak scattering. We discuss the possibility of topological superconductivity as an interpretation of these isotropic power-laws in conjunction with the anisotropic residual loss.

Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.title: Nontrivial Edge Superconductivity in Dirac Superconductor PdTe2
Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.authors: Bicong Ye, Zegang Liu, Tianyu Liu, Pingbo Chen, Jinhua Wang, Liang Zhou, Peiyao Qin, Hu Xu, Wenqing Zhang, Jiawei Mei, Jiannong Wang, Haizhou Lu, Hongtao He
Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.abstract: Superconducting topological materials with coexisted superconductivities and topological boundary states are promising platforms for realizing intrinsic topological superconductivity. In this work, the superconducting type-II Dirac semimetal PdTe2 is shown to exhibit clear periodic critical current oscillations in perpendicular magnetic fields due to the fluxoid quantization, indicating the existence of edge superconductivity in PdTe2. Furthermore, a comparative study of the different superconducting properties of the bulk and edge of PdTe2 provides direct evidence for this edge superconductivity. More importantly, by a careful analysis of the flux penetration area, the nontrivial character of the edge superconductivity is revealed, i.e., the edge superconductivity appears not only at the physical boundary of the flake, but also at the interior interface between superconducting and normal regions of PdTe2. The emergence of nontrivial edge superconductivity, indicative of the putative bulk topological superconductivity, not only reveals the great potential of PdTe2 but also provides an experimental avenue for exploring intrinsic topological superconductivity by leveraging bulk-boundary correspondence.

Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.title: Singlet-triplet superconductivity from repulsive interactions in a $p$-wave magnet
Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.authors: Hanbit Oh, Laura Classen, Daniel F. Agterberg
Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.abstract: Motivated by recent proposals of $p$-wave magnets, which host odd-parity spin splitting, we study electrons near Van Hove singularities with local repulsive interactions. We demonstrate how the symmetry of the $p$-wave spin splitting governs the competition among instabilities. Using a parquet renormalization group (pRG) analysis of a simple one-sublattice model of a $p$-wave magnet, we find that superconductivity is the leading instability over the entire phase diagram for purely repulsive interactions. The resulting superconducting state is generically a mixture of spin-singlet and spin-triplet pairing and approaches an equal-weight mixture when $T_c$ is small compared with the energy offset between each Van Hove electron and its inversion partner. Extending the pRG analysis to a more realistic two-sublattice model, we find that superconductivity remains the leading instability, while the sublattice degree of freedom leads to a competition among various singlet-triplet pairing channels and even a finite-momentum equal-spin pair-density wave. Our mechanism applies broadly to odd-parity magnets and opens a natural route to nodal topological superconductivity.

Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.title: Chiral Superconductivity Indifferent to Parent Topology in the Square-Lattice Hofstadter-Hubbard Model
Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.authors: Jia-Xin Zhang, Wen O. Wang, Leon Balents, Lucile Savary, D. N. Sheng
Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.abstract: We study a $π$-flux square-lattice $t$-$t'$ Hofstadter-Hubbard model proposed to be realizable in twisted moiré bilayers. By tuning $U$ and $t'$ at half filling, ground-state density-matrix renormalization group simulations (DMRG) and a parton analysis identify an integer quantum Hall (IQH) phase, a chiral spin liquid (CSL), and an antiferromagnet (AFM) in the phase diagram, while charge and spin fluctuations from finite-temperature determinant quantum Monte Carlo (DQMC) suggest a closing charge gap but an open spin gap at the IQH-CSL boundary, consistent with the topological criticality expected there. This model therefore produces a phase diagram hosting weakly correlated band topology (IQH), intrinsic topological order (CSL), and conventional symmetry breaking (AFM) side by side. Upon doping any of these three parent phases, a single chiral topological superconductor with spin Chern number $C_s=-2$ occupies nearly the entire phase diagram. DMRG, DQMC, and weak-coupling perturbation theory agree on its pairing symmetry. This shows that doping the topological band of our model robustly induces the same paired state throughout the phase diagram regardless of the character of the underlying correlated half-filled state and its magnetic fluctuations, whether an IQH, a spin liquid or a weakly fluctuating AFM.

Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.title: Topological phases and scattering protected by projective chiral symmetry
Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.authors: Théo Torres, Renaud Côte, Marc Pachebat, Antonin Coutant
Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.abstract: The bulk-boundary correspondence states that topological properties of a bulk material guarantee the existence of protected edge modes, oftentimes associated with the attractive property of backscattering immunity. In this Letter, we consider a time reversal invariant classical system with both translation and chiral, or sublattice, symmetries. We show that when these two symmetries anti-commute, the material exhibits a topological phase protected by the same invariant as type D topological superconductors. We realize such a system experimentally and observe the existence of the associated edge modes in an acoustic network. Our measurements are in excellent agreement with theoretical predictions from discrete lattice models. Finally, we show that these edge modes are immune to backscattering for perturbations consisting in two subsequent identical defects.

Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.title: Pressure-enhanced thermoelectric transport in layered Bi2Se3 through band structure optimization
Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.authors: Yuqi Gao, Dianzhen Wang, Shijie Hu, Dan Han, Jing Zou, Qiang Tao, Lu Wang, Yan Li, Pinwen Zhu
Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.abstract: In general, the pressure-optimized thermoelectric transport of 2D layered materials is attributed to strengthened interlayer interactions that reduce the bandgap. However, this also introduces a pronounced bipolar effect and band edge sharpening, thereby limiting thermoelectric performance. In this study, taking layered Bi2Se3 as an example, we observed the onset temperature of the bipolar effect from approximately 387 K at 1 GPa to 459 K at 5 GPa. First-principles calculations show that pressure-induced interlayer compression modifies the coupling between band edge pz orbitals, leading to an increase in the bandgap from 0.21 eV at ambient pressure to 0.292 eV at 5 GPa. This suppresses the bipolar effect and is accompanied by conduction band flattening, which increases the density-of-states effective mass and enhances the Seebeck coefficient. Additionally, the native Se vacancies in Bi2Se3 introduce donor levels, and pressure-induced modulation of these donor levels promotes carrier thermally excited, leading to an increased carrier concentration. This not only suppresses the bipolar effect but also compensates for the reduction in carrier concentration caused by the pressure-widened bandgap, maintaining high electrical conductivity, consequently resulting in a record-high power factor of 2663 μW·m−1·K−2 at 5 GPa, 580 K, and an estimated maximum ZT value of 0.804 at 5 GPa, 580 K. This study provides insights into pressure-induced band structure optimization for enhanced thermoelectric performance under high pressure.
